generator.program.note: The lineage's own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the herb base: it gives the values its species leave unset, which the herb program gave as defaults until then.

The order's woody program (growth plan G2.3a), on the broadleaf base: Apiaceae's own program grows its herbs, so its trees and shrubs take the order's, which gives the values its species leave unset, as the broadleaf program's defaults until then.

traits.inflorescence.note: Watson and Dallwitz's account of the family, as quoted in search results (the page itself was not read): flowers in umbels nearly always, or in heads. General accounts add that the umbel is usually compound, its rays ending in umbellets, as the family's old name, Umbelliferae, says; a simple umbel is less usual.

traits.note: Abrams's Illustrated Flora of the Pacific States, volume 3 (1951), read in full (Umbelliferae by Mathias and Constance): flowers small, epigynous; sepals usually 5, evident or often obsolete; petals 5 on the margin of the hypanthium, which is wholly adnate to the ovary (so no floral cup stands above it); stamens 5; ovary bicarpellate, 2-celled; outer flowers of an umbel sometimes radiant.

traits.woodiness.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), family 311 Umbelliferae: herbs, very rarely somewhat woody, with furrowed stems; leaves alternate, mostly much divided, sheathing at the base; fruit dry, splitting into two one-seeded halves (mericarps).

traits.leaf_arrangement.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), family 311 Umbelliferae: herbs, very rarely somewhat woody, with furrowed stems; leaves alternate, mostly much divided, sheathing at the base; fruit dry, splitting into two one-seeded halves (mericarps).

traits.leaf_division.note: Abrams (vol. 3, 1951, p. 215), Umbelliferae by Mathias and Constance: leaves alternate, compound or rarely simple, the petioles commonly dilated at the base. Hutchinson (1959) says the leaves are mostly much divided.

traits.division_pattern.note: Watson and Dallwitz (1992), Umbelliferae: compound leaves ternate, pinnate, bipinnate or more compound, palmate rarely; simple blades usually pinnatifid, palmatifid in Sanicula, Astrantia and Eryngium. A ternate leaf's leaflets are drawn along its midrib here, as cow parsnip's are.

traits.fruit_type.note: Hutchinson (vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1959), family 311 Umbelliferae: herbs, very rarely somewhat woody, with furrowed stems; leaves alternate, mostly much divided, sheathing at the base; fruit dry, splitting into two one-seeded halves (mericarps).

traits.stipules.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA), Umbelliferae: leaves usually without stipules, though some have stipule-like flanges; the Hydrocotyloideae have stipules.

traits.sexual_system.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA), Umbelliferae: plants usually with all flowers bisexual (about nine in ten); some andromonoecious or polygamomonoecious; dioecious in Acronema.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 431, 432, family Apiaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".
